paras: The Bayou Martin raid was an armed attack in August 1888 in which about 250 white men surprised Albert Narcisse, a Black man, and his brother in a field on Bayou Martin, nine miles from St. Martinsville, Louisiana, and fired on them after they fled to Narcisse's house. Narcisse and a ten-year-old boy were shot, the two men were captured, and the whites reported finding thirty new guns in the cabin. The main dispatch said the captives' fate was unknown, while one condensed version said Narcisse and his son had been fatally shot. Northern papers carried the report under headlines about Louisiana "race troubles" and whites "enraged" at Black residents arming themselves.

According to a St. Martinsville special that the Washington Critic credited to the New Orleans Picayune, local whites "had learned that the negroes were arming themselves with rifles," which were said to be hidden in Narcisse's house. The same dispatch placed the raid within a wider effort to disarm Black residents, reporting that whites above Breaux Bridge had called on them to surrender arms "which they have lately been getting together." The Sun ran the story under the headline "Another Fight Between Whites and Negroes in Louisiana."

About 250 whites came upon Narcisse and his brother in a field, "working" in most versions and "walking" in the Sun's. The two men ran to the house and tried to barricade it. The whites fired on the house, and the men surrendered after Narcisse and a ten-year-old boy had been shot. Inside the cabin, according to the whites' account, were thirty guns, "all new and heavily loaded with buckshot."

The fuller dispatch gives neither the boy's name nor his relation to Narcisse, and it does not say whether anyone in the house fired. A shorter New Orleans special described the episode as a "struggle" in which the whites seized the guns and Narcisse and "his son" were "fatally shot."

The dispatch ended by stating that it was not known what had been done with the two captured men. It also reported that further trouble was feared above Breaux Bridge, and the Sun's version added that Black residents there would probably not comply with the demand to give up their arms. No report of arrests, an inquest, or later news of Narcisse, his brother or the boy appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers outside Louisiana as a wire item, appearing on August 25 in the Rock Island Daily Argus, the Washington Critic and the New York Sun. Over the following ten days it was reprinted nearly word for word in the Middleburgh Post ("Surprised by the Whites"), the Hillsboro News-Herald, the Big Sandy News and the Ohio Democrat ("Race Troubles in Louisiana"), and the Somerset Herald ("War in Lousiana"). These texts called the raid an "encounter between negroes and whites," gave the whites' reason for it as fact, and presented the cache of guns as its result.

The Stark County Democrat's two-sentence version went further, opening with "a crowd of negroes" who had "secretly armed themselves" and treating the shooting as part of a struggle over the guns. By contrast, the Cleveland Gazette, which described itself as published "in the interest of the Colored People," reprinted the wire text on September 1 and followed it with a comment blaming "the Democrats." The Gazette wrote that suspicion that Black people were preparing to protect themselves against "Democratic outrages" had caused the "rebel alarm," and that "Negroes are killed if they resist foul attacks and they are shot down if they make no resistance." It closed by asking the Philadelphia Sentinel what defense it could offer for such outrages.

The reports disagree on the day: the Argus, the Critic, the Gazette and the Stark County Democrat say Tuesday afternoon, August 21, while the Sun says Thursday afternoon, August 23. They also differ on the outcome, since the fuller dispatch reports two people shot and the captives' fate unknown, while the condensed version reports Narcisse and his son fatally shot.

reader.title: Bayou Martin raid
bases: About 250 whites surprised two Black men, pursued them to a house, fired on it, shot two people and captured the men to seize a reported cache of guns (A2, A3, A4); no death is reported except in one condensed dispatch (A5).

A crowd of about 250 whites with no stated lawful authority attacked Narcisse's house on the claim that Black residents were arming (A2, A3, A4), but the fuller dispatch says only that Narcisse and a boy were shot and that the fate of the captured men was unknown (A2, A3); a single condensed dispatch says Narcisse and his son were 'fatally shot' (A5), so whether anyone was killed is unsettled.

Every account traces to one St. Martinsville special, which the Washington Critic attributes to the New Orleans Picayune (A4), reprinted in two textual variants (A2, A3) and condensed once (A5); no independent local report was found, and the account comes from the attackers' side.

accounts.label: Condensed New Orleans special
accounts.gist: A crowd of Black men at 'Martins Bayou' secretly armed; whites seized the guns in a struggle in which Narcisse and his son were fatally shot.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette editorial
accounts.gist: A suspicion that Black people were preparing to defend themselves against 'Democratic outrages' caused the 'rebel alarm'; Black people are killed if they resist and shot if they do not.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'The Louisiana Race Troubles' and 'Whites Enraged at the Blacks Arming Themselves' cast the raid as a race conflict provoked by Black arming, and the text states the whites' account as fact.
The Stark County Democrat's condensed version leads with Black men who 'secretly armed themselves' and calls the shooting a 'struggle' over the guns.
The Cleveland Gazette, a Black-owned weekly filed under the white-press collection, called the raid one of the 'outrages' of 'the Democrats' and challenged the Philadelphia Sentinel to defend it.

conflicts.note: Two text families of the same dispatch; the Tuesday version is carried by the paper that names the Picayune as source (A4), by the independent condensed dispatch (A5) and by most reprints, while only the Sun and the Somerset Herald (A11) print Thursday.
